a: Fungi communicate primarily through their mycelium — a vast, branching network of thread-like cells called hyphae that grows through soil, wood, and other substrates. The mycelium functions as a living information network, capable of sensing environmental conditions, transmitting signals across long distances, and coordinating colony-wide responses. One of the most extensively studied forms of fungal communication involves chemical signaling. Fungi release a wide array of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) into the soil and air, including terpenes, aldehydes, and ketones, which can be detected by other fungi, plants, bacteria, and even animals. These chemical messages serve diverse functions: they can attract insect vectors for spore dispersal, inhibit competing fungal species, or summon beneficial bacteria that assist in nutrient acquisition. Recent research has also revealed that fungi transmit electrical signals through their hyphae in patterns that resemble action potentials in neurons. A 2022 study by Andrew Adamatzky at the University of the West of England measured rhythmic electrical spikes propagating through fungal mycelia of several species, including enoki and split-gill mushrooms. These signals traveled at speeds of several millimeters per minute and displayed oscillatory patterns that varied in frequency and amplitude based on environmental stimuli. While it remains controversial whether these signals constitute a form of fungal "language," the electrical activity does appear to encode information about the fungus's state and surroundings. Within the mycelial network, fungi can also communicate through cytoplasmic streaming — the directed flow of cellular contents including nutrients, signaling molecules, and genetic material through the interconnected hyphal tubes. This allows a fungal colony to function almost as a distributed intelligence, where a stimulus detected at one point can trigger a coordinated metabolic response throughout the entire network. The discovery that fungal mycelia can solve complex spatial problems — such as finding the most efficient route through a maze to reach a food source — has led some researchers to describe the mycelial network as a form of distributed computation, analogous to the neural networks in animal brains but operating on vastly different time and spatial scales.

q: how do fungi talk to each other
how does the wood wide web work
a: The "Wood Wide Web" is the popular name for the mycorrhizal network, a symbiosis between fungi and plant roots that connects individual plants into an underground information and resource-sharing network. More than ninety percent of land plants form mycorrhizal associations, in which fungal hyphae envelop and penetrate plant root cells, creating a physical interface where nutrients and chemical signals are exchanged. The fungus delivers water, phosphorus, nitrogen, and other minerals that it extracts from the soil far more efficiently than plant roots can alone; in return, the plant supplies the fungus with carbohydrates produced through photosynthesis. This arrangement allows fungi to act as living cables linking the root systems of different plants, sometimes of entirely different species, into a shared network. Through these connections, trees and plants can transfer carbon, nutrients, and water to one another. Research by ecologist Suzanne Simard in Canadian forests demonstrated that paper birch and Douglas fir trees exchange carbon through shared mycorrhizal networks, with birches sending carbon to firs in the spring and fall when the firs are shaded, and firs returning the favor during summer when the birches are leafless. Beyond nutrient exchange, the mycorrhizal network enables plant-to-plant communication about environmental threats. When a plant is attacked by herbivores or infected by a pathogen, it can send chemical warning signals through the fungal network to neighboring plants, which then prime their own chemical defenses even before the threat directly reaches them. These signals include defense-related hormones such as jasmonic acid and salicylic acid, as well as volatile compounds. The fungal network also affects plant community dynamics: "mother trees" — the oldest, most connected trees in a forest — have been shown to preferentially channel resources through the network to their offspring seedlings, increasing their chances of survival. The structure of the mycorrhizal network is itself dynamic; fungi can sever connections with plants that fail to provide sufficient carbon, effectively sanctioning "cheaters." This complex system of mutual aid, signaling, and resource distribution has led scientists to describe forests not simply as collections of individual trees but as interconnected social networks, with fungi serving as the infrastructure that sustains communication and cooperation across the ecosystem.

While not true fungi — slime molds (Myxomycetes) are now classified in the kingdom Protista rather than Fungi — these remarkable organisms exhibit sophisticated communication and problem-solving abilities that have fascinated biologists and computer scientists alike. The best-studied species is Physarum polycephalum, the many-headed slime mold, which grows as a single giant cell containing millions of nuclei within a shared cytoplasm. This structure, called a plasmodium, extends a network of tubular veins that pulse rhythmically, contracting and expanding to shuttle cellular contents throughout the organism. Slime molds communicate internally through biochemical oscillations: the rhythmic contraction of the veins is controlled by chemical waves of calcium ions and ATP, which propagate through the cytoplasm and coordinate the movement and feeding behavior of the entire colony-like cell. When a slime mold is presented with a food source, it extends exploratory pseudopods in multiple directions, and the successful path is reinforced by increased cytoplasmic flow, while unsuccessful branches are pruned. This process allows the slime mold to solve complex spatial problems, including finding the shortest path through a maze and optimizing network designs that closely resemble human-engineered transportation systems. Japanese researchers demonstrated that a slime mold placed on a map of Japan with food sources at major cities created a network that closely matched the actual Tokyo rail system. Slime molds also communicate with the external environment through chemotaxis — they detect and move toward food odors and away from repellents — and can "remember" the location of food sources through the deposition of a slime trail that they avoid revisiting, a primitive form of externalized memory. Some species exhibit a form of habituation, a simple type of learning where they cease to respond to repeated harmless stimuli. While slime molds lack neurons or synapses, their intracellular signaling networks perform computational functions analogous to those of neural circuits, leading some researchers to argue that cognition is not exclusive to organisms with nervous systems. These findings challenge traditional definitions of intelligence and communication, suggesting that even single-celled organisms can process information, make decisions, and coordinate with their environment in ways we are only beginning to understand.
